articles.title: Princess Diana’s iconic ‘revenge dress’ by Christina Stambolian to be auctioned for up to $300,000; gown made history in 1994 and was last sold in 1997, two months before her death
articles.summary: UK News: Princess Diana’s iconic “revenge dress” is going under the hammer for the first time in nearly three decades, giving collectors another chance to own .
articles.body: Princess Diana’s iconic “revenge dress” is going under the hammer for the first time in nearly three decades, giving collectors another chance to own one of the most recognisable pieces of royal and fashion history.The legendary black silk evening gown, designed by Christina Stambolian, became a global pop-culture phenomenon when Diana wore it to a Vanity Fair dinner at London’s Serpentine Gallery on June 29, 1994 - the same day her then-husband, King Charles III, publicly admitted that he had been unfaithful during their marriage.More than 30 years after that unforgettable appearance, the dress will be auctioned by Sotheby’s in New York on December 9. It is estimated to fetch between $150,000 and $300,000, although its extraordinary cultural significance could potentially drive bidding higher.Why Princess Diana’s ‘revenge dress’ became so iconicDiana’s choice of outfit that night was far more than a fashion statement.The figure-hugging black silk dress featured an off-the-shoulder neckline, a dramatic side-swept train and a hemline above the knee - details that challenged traditional expectations surrounding royal fashion at the time.Diana paired the daring gown with black heels, a black clutch, bold red nails and a striking sapphire-and-diamond choker. According to Sotheby’s, the necklace was created from an antique diamond and sapphire brooch gifted to Diana by Queen Elizabeth, the Queen Mother, as a wedding present.The timing made the appearance even more powerful. Charles’ admission of infidelity had been revealed in an ITV documentary watched by around 13 million people across Britain.Rather than retreat from the intense media scrutiny surrounding her marriage, Diana stepped into the spotlight looking confident and self-assured - and the image quickly became one of the defining moments of her public life.‘Fashion can be a language when words fail’Morgane Halimi, Sotheby’s Global Head of Handbags and Fashion, said Diana instinctively understood the power of clothing.“Fashion can be a language when words fail or are simply not enough. Princess Diana understood that instinctively,” Halimi said in a statement.“She walked into a moment in which so much of her story was being told for her and, through what she chose to wear, reclaimed the narrative for herself,” she added.Halimi said the dress ultimately represented far more than the scandal surrounding the evening.“What has endured across the decades is not the scandal surrounding that evening, but Princess Diana’s show of confidence and self-possession,” she said.She also described the moment as a landmark in the history of fashion, saying it gave people — particularly women - permission to use clothing “as a shield, a weapon or both.”Diana almost didn’t wear the daring black gownInterestingly, the dress had been sitting in Diana’s wardrobe for around three years before its famous outing.Designer Christina Stambolian revealed in the 2013 Channel 4 documentary Princess Diana’s Dresses: The Auction that Diana had initially considered the design too daring.But on the night of the Vanity Fair dinner, she made the impulsive decision to wear it.Her former stylist Anna Harvey said Diana “wanted to look a million dollars” when she stepped out in the gown.The decision transformed what could have been another evening dress into an enduring symbol of independence and confidence.Princess Diana sold the dress months before her deathThe “revenge dress” was last sold in June 1997, when Diana auctioned 79 of her dresses to raise money for breast cancer and AIDS charities.The sale took place just two months before her death in a car crash in Paris on August 31, 1997.The dress was purchased by an unnamed couple and subsequently appeared at charity fundraising events in Scotland. It was later displayed at Paisley Museum, where it was last seen publicly nearly 30 years ago.A rare catalogue from Diana’s original 1997 dress auction will accompany the gown in the Sotheby’s sale. The catalogue credits Prince William with the sale’s design and was signed by both Diana and Stambolian.Anonymous owner explains why the dress is being soldThe current consignor, whose identity has not been disclosed, said the dress held enormous emotional significance for her and her late husband.“My late husband and I knew that this dress was something special. Princess Diana was walking into the worst night of her life and you would never know it to look at her,” the consignor said.“It went from a cocktail dress to a statement in the time it took to photograph her.”The owner added that winning the dress at auction had been one of the couple’s “great days” together.“With him gone, that chapter has closed, and so should this one,” the consignor said.She expressed hope that whoever ultimately buys the famous gown will enjoy owning it as much as she and her husband did.Could Princess Diana’s revenge dress sell for more than $300,000?Although Sotheby’s has estimated the gown at between $150,000 and $300,000, previous sales of Diana’s clothing suggest that collectors could push the final price considerably higher.One of Diana’s less famous dresses sold for $604,800 in 2023, dramatically exceeding its estimate.Her famous “Black Sheep” sweater also made headlines that year when it sold for more than $1.1 million, setting a record for one of Diana’s fashion pieces.The “revenge dress” carries an additional level of cultural significance because of the circumstances surrounding its most famous appearance, potentially making it one of the most closely watched Princess Diana fashion auctions in years.Where and when will Princess Diana’s revenge dress be displayed?Before the Sotheby’s auction in New York, the dress will travel internationally for public exhibitions.It will be unveiled at Sotheby’s London from September 18 to September 24, coinciding with London Fashion Week.It will then be displayed in Hong Kong from October 1 to October 15, followed by an exhibition in Geneva from November 6 to November 11.The gown will finally arrive in New York for the December 9 auction, with the exhibition beginning there on December 2.Some proceeds from the sale will be donated to NHS Lothian Charity on behalf of the Royal Edinburgh Hospital.Princess Diana’s revenge dress remains a cultural phenomenonThe black Christina Stambolian gown has remained deeply embedded in popular culture long after Diana’s death.Its image has been recreated in fashion, referenced across social media and featured in television portrayals of the late Princess of Wales, including Netflix’s The Crown.Its significance also goes beyond royal history. At a time when black was traditionally associated with mourning and was considered inappropriate for many royal occasions outside funerals, Diana’s choice helped turn the colour into an emblem of sophistication, confidence and personal freedom.Now, more than three decades after Diana first stepped out in the dress, the “revenge dress” is once again at the centre of global attention - this time as one of the most coveted pieces of Princess Diana memorabilia to reach the auction market.The sale also comes as Diana’s brother, Earl Spencer, prepares to publish Swan Song: Diana, My Sister, a book examining the life and legacy of his sister.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: OpenAI agents used 10+ sites for unsanctioned communication: Report
articles.summary: US News: WASHINGTON: AI agents unleashed by OpenAI used more than 10 previously undisclosed websites for unsanctioned communications earlier this year, accordi.
articles.body: WASHINGTON: AI agents unleashed by OpenAI used more than 10 previously undisclosed websites for unsanctioned communications earlier this year, according to six sets of independent investigators and data reviewed by Reuters, showing that the agents' rogue activity was wider ranging than previously disclosed.Although the behaviour falls short of hacking and is in some ways closer to spam, the revelation that OpenAI's agents circumvented their own restrictions to open communications channels on so many different sites - and that the company kept it quiet for months - may drive concerns both over the increasing capacity of AI models and the secrecy of the companies developing them.The scope of the agents' unauthorised communications was "somewhat larger than we thought it was," said Andrew Yoon, a researcher with the California nonprofit CivAI who said he tallied 18 previously undisclosed sites used by the agents between May and July. "It's almost certain that there's more going on here that we just don't know about."Last Friday, researchers reported that a swarm of agents from OpenAI hijacked a German-language wiki site.OpenAI did not directly address questions about how many different sites its agents used to communicate or say why it kept the activity under wraps for months. In a statement, it said it was undertaking a broader review of agent activity and had so far "not identified other activity matching the severity or scale of Hugging Face," a breach that drew global attention and raised concerns that OpenAI was losing control of its own technology. OpenAI added that it was working on a framework for reporting "misalignment" - industry-talk for rogue behavior - across training, evaluation, and deployment of AI models and would share it "soon."(This is a Reuters story)Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Canada and Ukraine boost cooperation on drone production
articles.summary: Canada and Ukraine are significantly expanding their cooperation on drone production, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney announced alongside Ukrainian Presi...
articles.body:
Canada and Ukraine have signed a new partnership to expand cooperation on drone production, aiming to equip the Canadian Armed Forces with world-leading capabilities and create jobs across Canada.

The collaboration between the two countries will cover all aspects of drone production, including critical metals, minerals, and engineering, with Canada planning to establish production capacity for "millions of drones" within the next two years.

In addition to drone production, Canada has pledged over $2 billion in assistance to Ukraine, including interceptor missiles for air defence, ammunition for Patriot air defence systems and F-16 fighter jets, and support for the energy sector and joint initiatives.

Canada and Ukraine are significantly expanding their cooperation on drone production, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney announced alongside Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky on Thursday.

"Today, Canada and Ukraine forged a new partnership which will equip the Canadian Armed Forces with world-leading drone capabilities, create jobs across Canada, and support Ukraine as they fight to achieve a just and lasting peace," Carney told a press conference in Calgary.

Cooperation between the two countries is to be expanded across all areas of drone production, "from critical metals and minerals to engineering," according to a statement.

Canada also aims to establish production capacity for "millions of drones" within the next two years. Carney said Canada currently has a total of 2,000 drones.

Carney also pledged further support for Ukraine, including interceptor missiles for air defence.

Zelensky said the assistance would include ammunition for Patriot air defence systems and F-16 fighter jets, as well as support for drone production.

"Overall, today's arrangements amount to more than $2 billion [US$1.45 billion] – including a government package of more than $1 billion for our defence, primarily to protect our skies: missiles for Patriots, munitions for F-16s, and drone coproduction. There are also arrangements for our energy sector and our joint initiatives," Zelensky said.

Twenty-one Ukrainian fighter pilots are currently being trained in Canada, Zelensky said.

"With the investments announced today, Canada's total commitments of multifaceted assistance for Ukraine have now reached over $26 billion since 2022," the Canadian government said.

Zelensky also thanked Canada for its willingness to participate in the development of the European Freyja missile defence system.

articles.title: Ukraine's fortress cities under fire as Russia bids to seize rest of Donbas
articles.summary: Kramatorsk and Slovyansk are now the main focus of Russian ground assaults, and residents are being told to leave.
articles.body:
It is so dangerous now in Slovyansk and Kramatorsk that police say it is time for civilians to get out. These neighbouring cities are the biggest still under full Ukrainian control in the eastern Donbas region.

In the worst affected areas, forced evacuations of families with children have already begun, says Pavlo Dyachenko of Donetsk police.

"This is the only way to save your life," he says, because security has deteriorated so much.

"If you take Slovyansk, it used to be hit by glide bombs roughly once a week, but now it's almost every day."

Slovyansk, Kramatorsk and Kostyantynivka, to the south, form part of what is known as Ukraine's "fortress belt" – a system of heavily reinforced defence lines in the east.

However, Kostyantynivka only has a limited presence of Ukrainian troops left, reports say, while Russia claims to be in full control of it.

The full capture of Donbas, made up of the Donetsk and Luhansk regions, is a key objective for Russia. Moscow has often cited the "liberation" and "protection" of the predominantly Russian-speaking Donbas as justification for the full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

The Russian army already controls almost all of Luhansk region, and is now in control of almost 80% of Donetsk region too, where all three fortress cities lie.

For the past few months, the territory near Kramatorsk and Slovyansk has been the main focus of Russian ground assaults. Capturing them would potentially make it much easier for Russia to advance to the west.

The two cities are now facing intense strikes from drones and bombs.

Many civilians have already left, and key streets there are now covered with anti-drone nets, says Viktor Makurin, a volunteer from London.

"There are often [remote-controlled] FPV drones in the air, you can hear them through the window. Driving around the city is lethally dangerous. There are drones lying in ambush on the roads, too," he told the BBC.

"You can always hear explosions in the background, plus there are mobile groups firing at drones."

Over the summer, the number of civilians wounded by Russian attacks on the two cities increased from 70 in June to 212 in August, say Ukrainian police.

Sixteen people died in June, 20 in July and 15 in August.

Residential housing comes under attack as well as infrastructure, says Dyachenko, causing "very significant destruction".

The number of glide bombs launched by Russia jumped from 40 in June to 109 in July and 92 in August, according to data published by Ukrainian police and studied by the BBC.

One morning two weeks ago, on 25 August, nine glide bombs targeted Kramatorsk. Seven hit civilian apartment blocks, wounding 24 people including a two-month-old baby, Ukrainian police say.

Two days later, it was hit again, this time with seven glide bombs, and five bombs targeted Slovyansk.

Fitted with winglets so they can glide to their target rather than fall, glide bombs are considered one of the most effective and lethal weapons in Russia's arsenal.

Usually, they weigh 250 or 500 kg, but there have been cases of Russia deploying bombs that weigh 1,500 kg.

"The devastation they cause is simply incredible," says Dyachenko.

"Glide bombs are the big fear," another British volunteer, John Auckland Abbey, posted on social media.

"They are silent killers, and when you've been abruptly woken by one exploding, you know at least another one will follow. The question you ask yourself as you lie very still in the dark is: will the next one be closer?"

Kramatorsk is currently home to the headquarters of the Donetsk regional administration. The capital city used to be Donetsk, until it was captured in 2014 by Russian-backed separatists.

What happens to the areas of Donbas still under Ukrainian control was reportedly a key issue when US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner visited Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky last weekend after their talks with Putin.

In the past, Witkoff has appeared to back Russian claims to the region, but Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky is refusing to pull troops out of it.

He says Putin has given his generals until the end of the year to complete their occupation of Donbas.

"Putin's primary objective on the front line remains the same: Kostyantynivka-Slovyansk," Zelensky told journalists last month.

Faced with mounting military pressure, the Ukrainian leader has created two new taskforces headed by experienced generals, Andriy Biletsky and Denys Prokopenko, to defend the portion of Donbas still in Ukrainian hands.

"There isn't just a battle for Donbas there," one unnamed Ukrainian general has said.

"What is probably the main battle of this year and the next is now unfolding."

articles.title: Charlie Kirk assassination allegedly mocked on campuses across country with celebrations, look-alike contests
articles.summary: Charlie Kirk lookalike contests and flyers mocking his death spread across campuses from Georgetown to NYU on the anniversary of his assassination.
articles.body: Celebrations and apparent Charlie Kirk "look-alike contests" are popping up on college campuses across the country on the first anniversary of the conservative activist’s assassination, with anonymous posts and flyers advertising events tied to Georgetown University, the University of South Carolina, the University of Maine, and New York University, among others. The latest apparent event surfaced in NYU’s Yik Yak community, where an anonymous user posted an image of a flyer advertising a "KIRKAVERSARY C. KIRK LOOKALIKE CONTEST" at "WSQ Park" at 10 p.m. Sept. 10, offering a $5 prize and instructing attendees to "BYOB." The NYU post followed similar apparent contests advertised through anonymous campus social media platforms at Georgetown in Washington, D.C., and the University of South Carolina, turning what initially appeared to be an isolated controversy into a broader phenomenon surrounding the anniversary of Kirk’s killing. DEMOCRATIC STUDENT GROUP TO PROTEST CHARLIE KIRK MEMORIAL AT CAMPUS WHERE HE WAS KILLED Kirk, the 31-year-old founder of Turning Point USA, was assassinated Sept. 10, 2025, while speaking at Utah Valley University during his "American Comeback Tour." Students at Georgetown University allegedly planned a Kirk "lookalike contest" for the anniversary of the conservative activist’s assassination, with the event drawing thousands of upvotes on Fizz, an anonymous social media platform popular with Georgetown students, according to screenshots shared with Fox News Digital from the school’s Turning Point USA chapter. Similarly, an apparent Kirk look-alike contest called "Kirkiversary" is being advertised at the University of South Carolina for Thursday. The screenshot featured an anonymous Yik Yak post circulating on social media advertising a "Charlie Kirk look-alike contest" on Greene Street outside USC’s Russell House at 7 p.m., offering a $50 prize and telling prospective participants, "Be there or be square." The University of South Carolina replied to the Libs of TikTok post saying, "We have no record of any registered student organization planning such an event. No university resources will be used to support this. DM us if you’d like a contact here that can help verify claims like this ahead of posting." Georgetown also told Fox News Digital that they were not tied to the event, saying, "We have seen no activity on campus related to these posts. Georgetown is not planning such an event and, to our knowledge, no student organization is hosting or planning such an event." REMEMBERING CHARLIE KIRK: TURNING POINT USA'S ANDREW KOLVET REFLECTS ON CONSERVATIVE GROUP'S CHALLENGING YEAR Other schools appear to be celebrating Kirk’s death, with images circulating on social media and shared by Libs of TikTok that appear to show flyers mocking Charlie Kirk’s death posted at the University of Nebraska-Lincoln. The flyers include an image of Kirk and the words "REST IN PISS FOREVER MISS" and "THE MASTERBAITER." A social media post circulating the images also claims that additional flyers have been posted around campus and that events celebrating Kirk’s death are being planned. The University of Tennessee-Knoxville also condemned messages that celebrate political violence after mysterious "Kirkaversery" [sic] flyers advertised a gathering apparently marking one year since Charlie Kirk’s assassination, declaring, "WE WILL CELEBRATE THE FIRST NEW YEAR AK (AFTER KIRK)." At Rochester Institute of Technology, flyers circulating online by Libs of TikTok appeared to advertise a "CHARLIE KIRK LOOKALIKE COMPETITION" at the Kate Gleason dorm quad on Sept. 10 at 1 p.m., with a prize listed as "$10 + FAME + TROPHY." The flyer did specify that the look-alike contest was not affiliated with RIT. A second flyer advertises a "Twerk for Kirk" competition with a $10 entry fee and monetary prizes. ERIKA KIRK URGES CONSERVATIVE STUDENTS NOT TO BACK DOWN IN FIRST SCHOOL YEAR SINCE CHARLIE'S ASSASSINATION Libs of TikTok also shared screenshots of a series of posts appearing in the University of Maine’s Yik Yak community on the first anniversary of Charlie Kirk’s assassination. Screenshots circulating online showed multiple anonymous posts using the term "Kirkiversary" and apparently mocking Kirk’s death and the manner in which he was killed. Among the posts visible in the screenshots are messages stating, "HAPPY KIRKIVERSARY!!!! TODAY IS A GREAT DAY!!!," "Carotid arteries out for Charlie Kirk!" and "Woke up with a horrible pain in my neck," accompanied by an image of a man experiencing neck pain. Similarly, purported internal messages attributed to members of the UNC Charlotte university community discussing the anniversary of Charlie Kirk’s assassination were also shared on X by Libs of TikTok. The messages, published on social media, appear to include individuals discussing how to celebrate the anniversary, joking about Kirk’s assassination and, in one instance, expressing hope that President Donald Trump would die. REPUBLICAN CONVENTION ATTENDEES SHARE HEARTFELT TRIBUTES TO LATE CHARLIE KIRK ON ASSASSINATION ANNIVERSARY In a statement to Fox News Digital, Wiley Norvell, senior vice president for university relations and public affairs at NYU, said, "No recognized student group is organizing any such event, nor is one taking place in an NYU building or space. University resources would never be used in this way. We are reporting these posts for misusing NYU's name. We strongly condemn any elevation of political violence." The University of Maine told Fox News Digital in a statement that the university "condemns violence, threats of violence and rhetoric that celebrates or makes light of violence in any form. The safety of our students, employees and visitors is a top priority. We take credible threats seriously, investigate them promptly and work with law enforcement and public safety partners when appropriate." The spokesperson continued, "The UMaine chapter of Turning Point USA held an event on campus Wednesday evening. The event was approved in advance and held in accordance with established university policies and procedures governing campus events. UMaine Police were present to support campus safety and security. The event concluded without incident and the university received no threats of violence associated with the event, either before, during or after it." The spokesperson added, "Yik Yak is an independent, third-party open and anonymous social media platform that is not affiliated with, sponsored by, endorsed by or administered by the University of Maine. The university does not operate or control the platform and does not have access to information identifying individuals behind anonymous posts. Any credible threat involving members of the university community or campus safety is taken seriously and addressed in accordance with university policies and established public safety procedures." CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE A UNC Charlotte spokesperson gave the following statement to Fox News Digital: "UNC Charlotte did not generate these messages. They were posted on Yik Yak, an anonymous third-party platform, and the University does not know who authored them. UNC Charlotte does not condone the posts. If the University receives credible information indicating that a member of our community has made a threat or violated University policy, we will review it and respond appropriately." A University of Nebraska-Lincoln spokesperson also addressed the controversy in comments to Fox News Digital. "The University of Nebraska–Lincoln is aware of flyers that were taped to bus stops on campus that contained imagery of the late Charlie Kirk. There is no indication that anyone affiliated with the university is responsible for the creation and/or distribution of the flyers," the spokesperson said. "The university does not condone or support messages making light of violence or the loss of life. The safety and well-being of our students, faculty, staff and visitors are our highest priority. The university encourages anyone who becomes aware of an immediate safety concern to report it through UNL Report or by calling University Police."
